entries.meaning: To arrange figures or facts in a table so that they can be compared. ---
examples: Volunteers tabulate the results overnight.
The clerk tabulated the votes twice.
We are still tabulating the survey answers.

entries.meaning: To fasten something in place with small nails or pins, or to change direction the way a sailboat does. ---
examples: Tack the poster to the bulletin board.
He tacked the schedule above his desk.
The campaign has been tacking toward the center all month.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she tacked the notice to the door), intransitive (the boat tacked into the wind)

entries.meaning: To follow someone closely and secretly in order to watch what they do. ---
examples: Two agents tail him everywhere he goes.
A reporter tailed the senator for a week.
She realized she was being tailed.

entries.meaning: To spoil the quality or the reputation of something by contact with something bad. ---
examples: One bad batch can taint a whole brand.
The scandal tainted his legacy for good.
The water was tainted with lead.

entries.meaning: To twist things together into a knotted mess that is hard to separate. ---
examples: These headphones tangle in my pocket every single time.
The wind tangled her hair on the way to school.
The kite string got tangled in the branches.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the wind tangled her hair), intransitive (these cords tangle easily)

entries.meaning: To fail or drop in value suddenly and badly. ---
examples: If the deal falls through, the shares will tank.
The movie tanked at the box office.
Sales have been tanking since the spring.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he tanked the interview), intransitive (the stock tanked)

entries.meaning: To tease someone by showing or promising something desirable that stays out of reach. ---
examples: Don't tantalize the dog with food he isn't allowed to have.
The smell of fresh bread tantalized the waiting crowd.
The offer was tantalizing enough to make her think twice.

entries.meaning: To give someone a particular job or duty to carry out. ---
examples: The mayor will task a small committee with the review.
They tasked her with rewriting the entire manual.
He has been tasked to report back by Friday.
entries.contrast: Usually passive, with with: be tasked with doing something.

entries.meaning: To mark the skin permanently with a design made with needles and ink. ---
examples: He wants to tattoo a compass on his forearm.
She tattooed her daughter's name on her wrist.
Both of his arms are heavily tattooed.

entries.meaning: To move unsteadily back and forth as if about to fall. ---
examples: The vase teeters on the edge of the shelf.
The company teetered on the brink of bankruptcy.
He was teetering on a ladder with a can of paint.
entries.contrast: Almost always used with on: teeter on the edge/brink of something.

entries.meaning: To grow one's first teeth, as a baby does. ---
examples: Babies usually start to teethe at around six months.
She teethed early and slept badly for weeks.
The baby is teething, so he chews on everything.
entries.contrast: The th here is voiced, as in breathe; the noun teeth ends in a hissing, voiceless th.

entries.meaning: To work from home by computer and phone instead of traveling to an office. ---
examples: Half the staff telecommute three days a week.
He telecommuted from Denver for all of last year.
Telecommuting saved her two hours of driving a day.

entries.meaning: To show what you are about to do before you do it, usually without meaning to. ---
examples: Good boxers never telegraph a punch.
His nervous glance telegraphed the answer.
The studio has been telegraphing the ending in every trailer.

entries.meaning: To speak to someone by phone. ---
examples: Please telephone the office before nine.
She telephoned twice and got no answer.
He is telephoning the hotel right now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (telephone the office), intransitive (she telephoned to cancel)
entries.contrast: In everyday American English call is far more common; telephone as a verb sounds formal or old-fashioned.

entries.meaning: To move instantly from one place to another without crossing the distance in between. ---
examples: In this game you can teleport back to base.
The crew was teleported down to the planet.
He kept teleporting behind me and winning the round.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the machine teleports objects), intransitive (the character teleports across the map)

entries.meaning: To make something less harsh or extreme by adding a moderating influence. ---
examples: Try to temper your criticism with a little praise.
Experience tempered his early optimism.
Her joy was tempered by worry about the cost.

entries.meaning: To offer or present something formally, such as a resignation or a payment. ---
examples: He plans to tender his resignation on Monday.
She tendered an apology in writing.
Payment must be tendered in full at the counter.

entries.meaning: To make meat softer by pounding it or soaking it in a marinade. ---
examples: A little acid will tenderize the beef.
He tenderized the steak with a mallet.
The chicken had been tenderized in buttermilk overnight.

entries.meaning: To tighten your muscles or go suddenly rigid, usually out of fear or effort. ---
examples: Try not to tense your shoulders when you lift.
She tensed the moment he said her name.
He could feel his jaw tensing.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he tensed his shoulders), intransitive (she tensed at the sound)

entries.meaning: To call something by a particular name or description. ---
examples: Economists term this a soft landing.
The judge termed the delay unacceptable.
What is loosely termed artificial intelligence covers many things.
entries.contrast: It takes two objects with no as: they termed the plan a failure, not termed the plan as a failure.

entries.meaning: To give evidence as a witness, usually in court and under oath. ---
examples: Three neighbors will testify for the defense.
She testified that she had never met the man.
He is testifying before the committee today.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (she testified that she saw him), intransitive (he testified at the trial)
entries.contrast: The -y changes to -ie-: testifies, testified.

entries.meaning: To feel a strong, urgent desire for something. ---
examples: Readers thirst for any detail about the case.
He thirsted for revenge for years.
A generation thirsting for change filled the square.
entries.contrast: Takes for: thirst for knowledge, never thirst something.

entries.meaning: To beat someone soundly, or to move about violently and wildly. ---
examples: They usually thrash us on our own field.
The swimmer thrashed at the water in panic.
A shark was thrashing in the shallows.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they thrashed the home team), intransitive (the fish thrashed in the net)
entries.contrast: A verb ending in -sh adds -es: he thrashes.

entries.meaning: To gather in or fill a place in a large crowd. ---
examples: Tourists throng the plaza every August.
Thousands thronged the cathedral for the service.
Shoppers were thronging the sidewalks by noon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (fans thronged the square), intransitive (crowds thronged to the gates)

entries.meaning: To choke someone by the throat, or to deliberately limit the speed or flow of something. ---
examples: Some carriers throttle your data after twenty gigabytes.
The provider throttled the connection at peak hours.
Video kept freezing because the network was throttling traffic.

entries.meaning: To hit something with a dull, heavy sound. ---
examples: Boxes thud onto the conveyor belt all day long.
The book thudded to the floor.
Her heart was thudding in her chest.
entries.русский: глухо стучать, ударяться с глухим звуком
entries.contrast: The final d doubles: thudded, thudding.

entries.meaning: To turn or handle pages with your thumb; also, to get a free ride by signaling with your thumb. ---
examples: Don't thumb the pages with wet hands.
She thumbed a ride all the way to Flagstaff.
He was thumbing the index, looking for my name.
entries.contrast: The b is silent: THUM.

entries.meaning: To hit or beat something heavily, making a dull sound. ---
examples: He thumps the table whenever he gets angry.
My heart thumped so loudly I could hear it.
Someone was thumping on the door at midnight.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (he thumped the table), intransitive (her heart thumped)

entries.meaning: To make the short, sharp sound a clock makes as it marks each second. ---
examples: You can hear the old clock tick from the hallway.
The meter ticked while we argued about the fare.
A bomb was ticking somewhere in the building.
entries.contrast: In American English you check a box on a form; tick a box is British.

entries.meaning: To give something a slight trace of a color or a feeling. ---
examples: A drop of beet juice will tinge the icing pink.
Her relief was tinged with guilt.
The sunrise was tingeing the clouds orange.
entries.contrast: The -ing form usually keeps the e to protect the soft g: tingeing.

entries.meaning: To make small changes to something in an attempt to repair or improve it. ---
examples: He likes to tinker with old radios on weekends.
Congress tinkered with the formula again.
She spent all Sunday tinkering with the engine.
entries.contrast: Takes with: tinker with something.

entries.meaning: To make a light, high ringing sound, like a small bell. ---
examples: The bells over the door tinkle whenever someone comes in.
Ice tinkled in the tall glass.
A piano was tinkling in the next room.

entries.meaning: To work long and hard at something exhausting. ---
examples: They toil in the fields from dawn to dusk.
She toiled for years over the manuscript.
Crews were toiling through the night to clear the road.

entries.meaning: To ring a bell slowly and repeatedly, especially to mark a death or an hour. ---
examples: The church bells toll every evening at six.
The bell tolled nine times for the fallen.
A single bell was tolling as the procession passed.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the sexton tolled the bell), intransitive (the bells tolled at noon)

entries.meaning: To deliberately set something on fire. ---
examples: Rioters threatened to torch the building.
Someone torched two cars overnight.
The warehouse had been torched for the insurance money.
entries.contrast: In American English a torch is a burning stick or a blowtorch; the battery-powered kind is a flashlight.

entries.meaning: To destroy something with a torpedo, or to deliberately ruin a plan or an agreement. ---
examples: A single senator could torpedo the whole bill.
A submarine torpedoed the tanker.
The talks were torpedoed by a leaked memo.
entries.contrast: The third-person form adds -es: he torpedoes it.

entries.meaning: To put a hand or another part of the body on something, or to come into contact with it. ---
examples: Please don't touch the paintings.
Her letter touched him deeply.
The plane's wheels were barely touching the runway.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (don't touch the screen), intransitive (their hands touched)
entries.contrast: A verb ending in -ch adds -es: she touches.

entries.meaning: To make something stronger or stricter, or to become so. ---
examples: Lawmakers want to toughen the penalties.
The city toughened its rules on short-term rentals.
Years at sea had toughened his hands.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the state toughened its laws), intransitive (his hands toughened over the summer)

entries.meaning: To praise something publicly and repeatedly in order to promote it. ---
examples: Officials tout the project as a model for the region.
He touted his experience in every interview.
The drug was widely touted as a breakthrough.

entries.meaning: To rise much higher than the things around it. ---
examples: The cranes tower over the old harbor.
He towered above his classmates by eighth grade.
A stack of files was towering on her desk.
entries.contrast: Takes over or above: tower over the crowd.

entries.meaning: To consider an idea casually, or to handle something idly without real attention. ---
examples: I toy with the idea of moving every winter.
She toyed with her food and said nothing.
He has been toying with the notion of retiring early.
entries.русский: играть (с мыслью), забавляться; вертеть в руках
entries.contrast: Takes with: toy with an idea.

entries.meaning: To register a name, logo, or phrase legally so that only you may use it. ---
examples: They tried to trademark the phrase "game day".
The company trademarked the shape of the bottle.
The slogan is trademarked in forty countries.

entries.meaning: To walk or wander about in a tired, aimless, or irritating way. ---
examples: I'm not going to traipse across town in this rain.
We traipsed through three museums in one afternoon.
Kids kept traipsing through the kitchen in muddy boots.

entries.meaning: To give a drug that makes a person or an animal calm or unconscious. ---
examples: Rangers had to tranquilize the bear.
The horse was tranquilized before the flight.
They are tranquilizing the elephant so they can move her.
entries.contrast: American English uses one l: tranquilize, tranquilized; British English writes tranquillise.

entries.meaning: To carry out business or an exchange of money with someone. ---
examples: Most customers now transact entirely online.
The firm transacted millions in trades that morning.
Business was transacted in three languages.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (transact business), intransitive (most customers transact online)

entries.meaning: To go beyond the usual limits of something. ---
examples: Great music can transcend language.
Her appeal transcended party lines.
The issue has long since transcended local politics.

entries.meaning: To hold someone's attention so completely that they cannot move or look away. ---
examples: The final scene will transfix you.
The verdict transfixed the courtroom.
The children stood transfixed by the fire.

entries.meaning: To break a rule, a law, or a moral boundary. ---
examples: Artists like to transgress the usual boundaries.
He knew he had transgressed an unwritten rule.
Anyone transgressing the policy will be suspended.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (transgress the rules), intransitive (those who transgress are punished)

entries.meaning: To happen, or to become known after having been secret. ---
examples: No one knows what will transpire at the hearing.
It later transpired that the email had been deleted.
Nothing of interest has transpired since Monday.

entries.meaning: To cause someone lasting emotional shock or injury. ---
examples: Don't let one bad teacher traumatize you.
The crash traumatized everyone on board.
He was traumatized by what he saw during the flood.

entries.meaning: To travel or move across an area, especially a large or difficult one. ---
examples: The trail traverses three states.
They traversed the glacier in two days.
A new bridge traversing the canyon opens in May.

entries.meaning: To search through a large quantity of material for what you want, or to fish by dragging a net. ---
examples: Investigators trawl social media for leads.
She trawled the archives for his letters.
Two boats were trawling just off the coast.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they trawled the archives), intransitive (the boats trawl for shrimp)

entries.meaning: To become widely talked about online, or to move steadily in a general direction. ---
examples: Anything about the finale will trend by morning.
The hashtag trended worldwide for two days.
Prices have been trending downward since March.

entries.meaning: To locate a position or establish the truth by combining measurements or sources taken from different angles. ---
examples: Two towers are enough to triangulate a phone.
Police triangulated the signal to a motel outside town.
We are triangulating the estimates against census data.
entries.русский: определять методом триангуляции; сопоставлять (данные из разных источников)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (police triangulated his location), intransitive (the candidate triangulates between the two camps)

entries.meaning: To treat someone or something without the seriousness they deserve. ---
examples: She is not a woman to trifle with.
He trifled with her feelings for a year.
You are trifling with a very dangerous man.
entries.contrast: Takes with, and is heard most often in the negative: not to be trifled with.

entries.meaning: To make something serious look small or unimportant. ---
examples: Please don't trivialize what she went through.
The coverage trivialized a real public health problem.
He has a habit of trivializing other people's fears.
entries.contrast: American spelling keeps -ize; British writes trivialise.

entries.meaning: To post deliberately provocative or mocking messages online in order to upset someone. ---
examples: Some accounts troll every post the mayor puts up.
He trolled the comment section for an hour and then deleted everything.
She was trolled so badly that she left the platform.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (troll a celebrity), intransitive (he was only trolling)

entries.meaning: To walk somewhere together as a group. ---
examples: Every morning the kids troop into the gym for announcements.
The whole family trooped out to the car in the rain.
Fans were already trooping toward the stadium at noon.
entries.русский: идти гурьбой, идти толпой; шагать группой
entries.contrast: The noun troops means soldiers; the verb only means to walk somewhere in a bunch.

entries.meaning: To walk slowly and heavily because you are tired or the ground is hard going. ---
examples: We trudge up that hill twice a day.
She trudged through the snow to the mailbox.
They were trudging home with the last of the boxes.

entries.meaning: To announce something loudly and proudly. ---
examples: Politicians trumpet every job they help create.
The company trumpeted record profits the same week it cut staff.
The findings are being trumpeted as a breakthrough.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (trumpet the results), intransitive (an elephant trumpeted in the dark)
entries.contrast: No doubled t: trumpeted, trumpeting — the stress is on the first syllable.

entries.meaning: To shorten something by cutting off its end. ---
examples: Spreadsheets often truncate long text without warning.
The broadcast truncated her answer at the worst possible moment.
The list has been truncated to the first ten results.

entries.meaning: To move, or push something, slowly and heavily on wheels. ---
examples: Freight trains trundle past the house all night.
He trundled a wheelbarrow of bricks across the yard.
An old school bus came trundling up the hill.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (trundle a cart down the hall), intransitive (the truck trundled past)

entries.meaning: To dig a passage under or through something. ---
examples: Moles tunnel under the whole lawn every spring.
The prisoners tunneled forty feet before anyone noticed.
Crews are tunneling beneath the river for the new subway line.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tunnel a passage), intransitive (tunnel under the wall)
entries.contrast: American English keeps one l: tunneled, tunneling; British doubles it: tunnelled, tunnelling.

entries.meaning: To give something a sudden, powerful boost. ---
examples: Tax breaks can turbocharge a local economy.
Cheap credit turbocharged the housing market.
The campaign has been turbocharged by one viral video.
entries.русский: резко ускорять, форсировать; придавать мощный импульс
entries.contrast: Literally it means to fit an engine with a turbocharger: a turbocharged four-cylinder.

entries.meaning: To struggle or fight with someone, usually briefly and without weapons. ---
examples: The two boys tussle over the same toy every afternoon.
Protesters tussled with officers at the gate.
The two agencies have been tussling over the budget for months.
entries.contrast: You tussle with a person and over the thing you are fighting about.

entries.meaning: To post a short public message on social media. ---
examples: He tweets about the team after every game.
She tweeted a photo of the line outside the store.
The mayor has been tweeting through the whole storm.
entries.русский: писать в соцсетях, твитнуть; постить короткое сообщение
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tweet a photo), intransitive (he tweets all day)
entries.contrast: The older meaning is the sound a small bird makes: sparrows tweeting outside the window.

entries.meaning: To pull out hairs or small objects with tweezers. ---
examples: She tweezes her eyebrows in front of the bathroom mirror.
He tweezed the splinter out of my thumb.
Stop tweezing — it grows back unevenly.

entries.meaning: To turn or twist something idly with your fingers. ---
examples: He twiddles a pen the whole time he is on the phone.
She twiddled the dial until the static cleared.
We sat twiddling our thumbs for two hours.
entries.contrast: Twiddle your thumbs means to sit doing nothing while you wait.

entries.meaning: To make a small sudden movement that you cannot control. ---
examples: My left eye twitches when I don't sleep.
The dog's ear twitched at the sound of the bag.
His hands were twitching from too much coffee.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the rabbit twitched its nose), intransitive (her eyelid twitched)
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -ch: twitches.

entries.meaning: To make the light, quick sounds of small birds. ---
examples: Sparrows twitter in the hedge all morning.
Birds twittered somewhere above the parking lot.
We woke to a whole tree twittering outside the window.
entries.contrast: The social network took its name from this verb, but for posting online the verb is tweet.

entries.meaning: To be a typical example of something. ---
examples: These two songs typify everything the band did well.
His answer typified the company's attitude toward complaints.
That mix of charm and chaos has typified the city for a century.
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ies and -ied: typifies, typified.

entries.meaning: To rule or treat people cruelly and unfairly. ---
examples: Petty bosses tyrannize small offices.
He tyrannized his staff for twenty years and called it discipline.
The valley had been tyrannized by one family for generations.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (tyrannize a household), intransitive (tyrannize over the weak)
entries.contrast: Double n, like tyranny — but tyrant has only one.

entries.meaning: To make something lose its balance or its even proportions. ---
examples: One heavy box can unbalance the whole load.
The extra weight unbalanced the canoe and we went over.
The roster looked unbalanced after the trade.
entries.русский: выводить из равновесия, вывести из равновесия; нарушать равновесие

entries.meaning: To clear something that is blocked, or to let a blocked person contact you again. ---
examples: Plumbers unblock a hundred drains a week in this neighborhood.
She unblocked him after a month of silence.
The road has finally been unblocked.

entries.meaning: To take a new product out of its packaging, often on camera. ---
examples: Reviewers unbox every new phone the day it ships.
He unboxed the console live for forty thousand viewers.
She is unboxing the camera in the next video.
entries.contrast: After -x the third person takes -es: unboxes.

entries.meaning: To separate things that used to be sold or offered together as one package. ---
examples: Carriers now unbundle channels so you pay only for what you watch.
The airline unbundled seat selection from the ticket price.
Services that were once sold together are being unbundled one by one.
entries.русский: разделять (пакет услуг), разукрупнять; продавать по отдельности

entries.meaning: To tell someone your worries so that you feel lighter. ---
examples: People unburden themselves to strangers on long flights.
She finally unburdened herself to her sister.
He left the room looking unburdened for the first time in weeks.
entries.русский: изливать душу, излить душу; облегчать душу, снимать бремя
entries.contrast: Usually reflexive and followed by to: unburden yourself to a friend.

entries.meaning: To click a checked box on a screen so that it is no longer selected. ---
examples: Uncheck the box if you don't want their newsletter.
I unchecked every option and started over.
Two settings had been unchecked by the update.
entries.contrast: As an adjective unchecked means uncontrolled: unchecked spending.

entries.meaning: To pull the cork out of a bottle. ---
examples: They uncork something good every New Year's Eve.
He uncorked the wine and let it sit for an hour.
The champagne had already been uncorked when we arrived.

entries.meaning: To do less well than you are able to. ---
examples: Bright students sometimes underachieve out of boredom.
The team underachieved all season and fired the coach in March.
He has been underachieving since the move.
entries.русский: не реализовывать свой потенциал, работать (учиться) ниже своих возможностей

entries.meaning: To ask someone for less money than the correct price. ---
examples: Small repair shops often undercharge for labor.
The waiter undercharged us by twenty dollars.
We had been undercharged for two years before anyone noticed.
entries.русский: брать меньше положенного, недобирать плату; занижать цену
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (they undercharged me), intransitive (that shop undercharges)

entries.meaning: To cook food for too short a time, so that it is not done in the middle. ---
examples: Cheap ovens undercook the middle of everything.
He undercooked the chicken and we ordered pizza instead.
Nothing ruins a plate faster than an undercooked potato.
entries.русский: недоваривать, недожаривать; не доводить до готовности

entries.meaning: To dress more casually than the occasion calls for. ---
examples: I always underdress for weddings.
She underdressed for the interview and felt it the whole hour.
Everyone else was in a suit and I was badly underdressed.
entries.contrast: You usually meet it as be underdressed: he was underdressed for the funeral.

entries.meaning: To think something is smaller, easier, or less important than it really is. ---
examples: Never underestimate how long a move takes.
They badly underestimated the cost of the repairs.
Her influence on the team has been underestimated for years.
entries.contrast: The verb ends in a full vowel, un-dur-ES-tuh-mayt; the noun an underestimate ends in a schwa, un-dur-ES-tuh-muht.

entries.meaning: To give a program or an organization less money than it needs. ---
examples: States underfund rural hospitals year after year.
Congress underfunded the agency and then blamed it for the delays.
The after-school program has been underfunded since day one.

entries.meaning: To give a person or an animal less food than they need to stay healthy. ---
examples: Two bad harvests can undernourish a whole region.
The drought undernourished a generation of children.
The puppies had been badly undernourished before the shelter took them.
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es after -sh: undernourishes.

entries.meaning: To do worse than expected, or worse than whatever you are compared with. ---
examples: The older stores underperform in every quarter but December.
The fund underperformed the market three years running.
Two of the three plants are underperforming.
entries.русский: показывать слабые результаты, отставать; работать хуже ожидаемого
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the fund underperformed the index), intransitive (the team underperformed)

entries.meaning: To think someone or something is less good or less important than it really is. ---
examples: Coaches underrate players from small schools.
Critics underrated the album when it came out.
That diner is the most underrated place in town.
entries.contrast: Double r: the prefix under- ends in r and rate begins with one — underrated, not underated.

entries.meaning: To state a number as lower than it really is. ---
examples: Restaurants underreport tips every April.
The agency underreported the number of cases for months.
Assaults on nurses are chronically underreported.
entries.contrast: Double r, and it is often hyphenated: under-report.

entries.meaning: To give a group of people less service than they need. ---
examples: Broadband companies underserve small towns.
The old bus map underserved the entire east side.
The clinic was built for underserved families.
entries.русский: недостаточно обслуживать, не обеспечивать нужными услугами

entries.meaning: To run a place with fewer workers than it needs. ---
examples: Chains understaff their stores on purpose.
Management understaffed the night shift all summer.
The emergency room is badly understaffed on weekends.
entries.русский: недоукомплектовывать штат, не обеспечивать достаточным персоналом

entries.meaning: To describe something as smaller or less serious than it really is. ---
examples: Insurance forms understate what a total loss really costs.
He understated the damage to keep everyone calm.
To call the drive long would be understating it.

entries.meaning: To use something much less than it could be used. ---
examples: Cities underutilize the buildings they already own.
The company underutilized its best engineers for a decade.
Half the equipment sits underutilized in a locked room.
entries.русский: использовать не в полную силу, недоиспользовать
entries.contrast: Also written under-utilize; the plainer underuse means the same thing.

entries.meaning: To treat something or someone as worth less than they really are. ---
examples: Employers still undervalue work done at home.
The bank undervalued the house by sixty thousand dollars.
She felt undervalued and left after a year.

entries.meaning: To disappoint someone by being far less impressive than expected. ---
examples: Sequels usually underwhelm the people who loved the original.
The new phone underwhelmed the reviewers.
We came out of the show thoroughly underwhelmed.
entries.русский: разочаровывать, не впечатлять; не оправдывать ожиданий
entries.contrast: Coined as a joke on overwhelm, and still its everyday opposite.

entries.meaning: To move or lie in smooth waves. ---
examples: Fields of wheat undulate all the way to the highway.
The water undulated under the dock.
We drove for an hour through undulating farmland.

entries.meaning: To dig something up, or to find information that was hidden. ---
examples: Winter storms often unearth old coins along this beach.
Reporters unearthed three years of unpaid fines.
A crew is unearthing the foundation of the original church.

entries.meaning: To stop seeing someone's posts by removing them from the accounts you follow. ---
examples: People unfollow accounts that post ten times a day.
She quietly unfollowed half her coworkers.
He has been unfollowing anyone who argues in the replies.
entries.contrast: Unfollow is not block: unfollowing only hides the posts, it does not cut the person off.

entries.meaning: To unroll and spread out something that was rolled or folded, such as a flag or a sail. ---
examples: Cadets unfurl the flag at sunrise.
The crew unfurled the sail as soon as the wind picked up.
A banner was unfurled from the upper deck.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (unfurl a banner), intransitive (the sail unfurled)

entries.meaning: To make someone lose their emotional balance or self-control. ---
examples: Grief like that can unhinge a person.
Months of harassment slowly unhinged him.
By then the pressure had unhinged her completely.
entries.contrast: Most often met as the adjective unhinged, meaning wild or out of control: an unhinged rant.

entries.meaning: To free something from the hook, rope, or coupling that holds it. ---
examples: Give me a hand and we'll unhitch the trailer.
He unhitched the horse and led it into the barn.
They were unhitching the boat when the rain started.

entries.meaning: To bring separate parts or groups together into a single whole. ---
examples: A common threat can unify a divided country.
The new coach unified a locker room full of egos.
They are unifying three separate databases into one.
entries.contrast: Consonant + -y changes: unify → unifies, unified, but unifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To form a labor union, or to organize workers into one. ---
examples: The baristas voted to unionize last spring.
Two more warehouses unionized this month.
Organizers have been unionizing stores across the state.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (unionize a warehouse), intransitive (the drivers unionized)
entries.contrast: American unionize; British writing has unionise.

entries.meaning: To open something by releasing the latch that holds it shut. ---
examples: Don't unlatch the gate — the dog will run off.
She unlatched the window to let some air in.
He was unlatching the toolbox when his phone rang.

entries.meaning: To release something powerful that has been held back. ---
examples: The ruling could unleash a flood of lawsuits.
The storm unleashed six inches of rain in one night.
The video has unleashed a wave of criticism.

entries.meaning: To reveal the true identity or true nature of someone or something. ---
examples: Two reporters set out to unmask the anonymous blogger.
A DNA test finally unmasked the killer.
The film is unmasking a fraud that lasted thirty years.

entries.meaning: To make someone lose confidence and feel nervous or frightened. ---
examples: Empty hallways at night unnerve me.
The silence in the courtroom unnerved the witness.
There was something unnerving about how calm he stayed.
entries.contrast: Two ns, because it is un + nerve: unnerve, unnerved.

entries.meaning: To open something that is rolled up, or to come open in that way. ---
examples: Unroll your mat and find a spot.
He unrolled the blueprints across the table.
The banner was slowly unrolling down the side of the building.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (unroll the mat), intransitive (the carpet unrolled across the floor)

entries.meaning: To turn something mixed up or coded back into clear, ordered form. ---
examples: Can you unscramble these letters into a city name?
The receiver unscrambled the signal instantly.
She spent the morning unscrambling the numbers in the report.

entries.meaning: To open or remove something by turning it, or by taking out its screws. ---
examples: Unscrew the cap slowly — the bottle is warm.
He unscrewed the burned-out bulb and put in a new one.
I was unscrewing the back panel when the battery fell out.

entries.meaning: To open something closed with a seal, especially sealed court records. ---
examples: A judge agreed to unseal the indictment.
They unsealed the envelope in front of two witnesses.
The documents were unsealed on Friday morning.

entries.meaning: To remove someone from a position of power, especially by beating them in an election. ---
examples: She is running to unseat a four-term congressman.
A political newcomer unseated the mayor in November.
No challenger has ever unseated him in a primary.
entries.русский: смещать (с поста), сместить; свергать, выбивать из седла

entries.meaning: To make someone feel anxious or uneasy. ---
examples: The news seemed to unsettle everyone in the office.
His quiet voice unsettled her more than shouting would have.
There is something unsettling about this whole arrangement.

entries.meaning: To separate things that are twisted together, or to make a confusing situation clear. ---
examples: It takes five minutes to untangle these cords every morning.
Lawyers untangled the contract line by line.
She is still untangling her mother's finances.

entries.meaning: To pull out cloth that has been tucked in, such as a shirt or a bed sheet. ---
examples: Untuck your shirt if you want to look less formal.
He untucked his shirt the second the meeting ended.
The kids had untucked every sheet on the bed by morning.

entries.meaning: To criticize someone sharply for something they have done. ---
examples: She is not afraid to upbraid her own staff in public.
The senator upbraided the agency for its slow response.
He stood at the rail, upbraiding the referee.
entries.contrast: You upbraid someone for something. It is formal; in speech Americans say scold or chew out.

entries.meaning: To turn something old or thrown away into something of greater value. ---
examples: They upcycle old pallets into garden furniture.
She upcycled a wooden ladder into a bookshelf.
The shop specializes in upcycling vintage denim.
entries.русский: перерабатывать во что-то лучшее, давать вторую жизнь (вещи)
entries.contrast: Recycle breaks a thing down into raw material; upcycle keeps it whole and makes it better.

entries.meaning: To turn something over on its end, or to overturn a settled situation. ---
examples: One ruling could upend the whole industry.
The move upended our plans for the year.
Cheap streaming is upending the way studios make money.
entries.русский: переворачивать (вверх дном), опрокидывать; ломать привычный порядок

entries.meaning: To cover a chair or sofa with padding and fabric. ---
examples: They can upholster the chair in any fabric you choose.
We upholstered the old sofa in green velvet.
The booths are upholstered in cracked red leather.

entries.meaning: To draw attention away from someone who should be the center of it. ---
examples: Nobody wants to upstage the bride.
The opening act completely upstaged the headliner.
He has a talent for upstaging his own colleagues.
entries.русский: затмевать, затмить; перетягивать внимание на себя

entries.meaning: To mark an online post or comment as good so that more people see it. ---
examples: If this helped, upvote it.
Thousands of readers upvoted the comment overnight.
Her answer has been upvoted more than any other on the site.
entries.contrast: The opposite is downvote. Drop the e before -ing: upvoting.

entries.meaning: To turn rural land into a city area, or to become one. ---
examples: Cheap land is helping urbanize the whole valley.
China urbanized faster than any country in history.
The county has been rapidly urbanizing since the 1990s.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (urbanize the valley), intransitive (the region urbanized quickly)
entries.contrast: American urbanize; British urbanise. The noun is urbanization.

entries.meaning: To pass urine from the body. ---
examples: Patients are asked to urinate in a cup before the exam.
The dog urinated on the rug again.
Urinating more often than usual can be an early sign.
entries.contrast: A clinical word. In everyday speech Americans say pee; urinate belongs in a doctor's office or a police report.

entries.meaning: To put something to work for a purpose. ---
examples: Can I use your phone for a minute?
We used the last of the milk this morning.
She has been using the same laptop for six years.
entries.contrast: The verb use ends in a z sound (YOOZ); the noun use and the phrase used to end in an s sound (YOOS, YOOS-tuh). Drop the e before -ing: using.

entries.meaning: To take power, a position, or a right from someone without having the authority to do so. ---
examples: A general tried to usurp the throne.
The committee gradually usurped powers that belonged to the mayor.
He was accused of usurping his brother's title.

entries.meaning: To make practical use of something, especially a resource. ---
examples: The kitchen utilizes every scrap of donated food.
We utilized an empty warehouse as a studio.
The lab is utilizing a new imaging technique.
entries.contrast: American utilize, British utilise. In ordinary sentences plain use sounds better; utilize is business and technical English.

entries.meaning: To spend a vacation in a particular place. ---
examples: They usually vacation on the Oregon coast.
We vacationed in Maine last August.
The family has been vacationing there for thirty years.
entries.contrast: An American verb. British English keeps holiday and says go on holiday.

entries.meaning: To keep changing your mind instead of making a decision. ---
examples: He tends to vacillate whenever money is involved.
The board vacillated for months before picking a site.
She kept vacillating between the two job offers.
entries.contrast: You vacillate between two choices. One c, two ls: vacillate.

entries.meaning: To disappear suddenly and completely. ---
examples: Towns like this one simply vanish from the map.
My keys vanished somewhere between the car and the door.
The snow was vanishing fast in the afternoon sun.
entries.contrast: Third person adds -es: vanishes. It takes no object — things vanish, but you cannot vanish something.

entries.meaning: To defeat an enemy or an opponent completely. ---
examples: The hero sets out to vanquish the dragon.
Their team vanquished the defending champions.
He has vanquished every rival in the state.
entries.contrast: Literary and formal. In ordinary American speech the word is beat or defeat.

entries.meaning: To inhale vapor from an electronic cigarette. ---
examples: You can't vape inside the building.
He vaped through the entire flight.
The school has a problem with students vaping in the bathrooms.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (vape mint pods), intransitive (he vapes on the porch)

entries.meaning: To sell goods, especially from a machine, a stall, or a cart. ---
examples: The machines in the lobby vend snacks and cold drinks.
He vended newspapers on that corner for thirty years.
Hot coffee is vended from a kiosk near the gate.
entries.contrast: The everyday word is sell; vend survives mainly in vending machine and in formal or legal writing.

entries.meaning: To regard someone or something with deep respect, often as sacred. ---
examples: Many cultures venerate their ancestors.
Students venerated the old professor long after he retired.
The shrine is venerated by pilgrims from three religions.

entries.meaning: To go somewhere risky, or to offer an opinion at the risk of being wrong. ---
examples: Few hikers venture this far up the canyon in winter.
She ventured a guess at what the repair would cost.
Nobody has ventured an opinion since the argument started.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (venture a guess), intransitive (few hikers venture this far)

entries.meaning: To put a thought or feeling into words. ---
examples: Try to verbalize what is actually bothering you.
He never verbalized his objection, but everyone could see it.
She was verbalizing every step as she solved the problem.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (verbalize your fears), intransitive (children verbalize before they read)
entries.contrast: American spelling verbalize; British verbalise.

entries.meaning: To come so close to a state or quality that it almost becomes it. ---
examples: His confidence verges on arrogance.
The mood of the crowd verged on panic.
Her patience was verging on exhaustion by the third hour.
entries.contrast: Needs on or upon: verge on collapse, never verge collapse.

entries.meaning: To give someone a legal right or power, or, of such a right, to take full effect. ---
examples: Half of her stock options vest next spring.
The title vested automatically when the trust closed.
Employees are fully vested in the pension after five years.
entries.русский: переходить в собственность, вступать в силу; наделять (правом)
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the charter vests the mayor with veto power), intransitive (the shares vest in March)

entries.meaning: To treat someone unfairly or single them out for harm. ---
examples: Scammers victimize older people with fake phone calls.
The report found that whistleblowers had been victimized for speaking up.
He was convinced the whole system was victimizing him.
entries.contrast: American spelling victimize; British victimise.

entries.meaning: To compete eagerly with others for something. ---
examples: Six candidates vie for two open seats.
The studios vied for the rights to her first novel.
Three teams are vying for the last playoff spot.
entries.contrast: The -ing form is vying, not vieing.

entries.meaning: To attack someone's reputation with harsh, unfair criticism. ---
examples: Talk shows vilify whoever is convenient that week.
He was vilified in the press for months.
Stop vilifying people you have never met.
entries.contrast: The -y changes: vilifies, vilified, but vilifying.

entries.meaning: To clear someone of blame, or to prove that a claim was right after all. ---
examples: The new evidence should vindicate him.
The audit vindicated her warnings about the budget.
He has been fully vindicated by the court.

entries.meaning: To record and post short personal videos online. ---
examples: He vlogs about cooking on the weekends.
She vlogged the entire road trip from Denver to the coast.
They have been vlogging since high school.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (vlog the whole trip), intransitive (she vlogs every week)
entries.contrast: The g doubles: vlogged, vlogging — as in blog.

entries.meaning: To express something out loud, in words or in sounds. ---
examples: Few employees vocalize their doubts in front of the boss.
She finally vocalized what everyone had been thinking.
The chimps were vocalizing from the far side of the enclosure.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (vocalize a complaint), intransitive (the baby vocalizes constantly)

entries.meaning: To show a formal choice in an election or a group decision. ---
examples: Most residents now vote by mail.
She voted early on Tuesday morning.
Only a third of the students had voted by noon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the board voted him chairman), intransitive (vote by mail)
entries.contrast: You vote for a person but vote on a proposal.

entries.meaning: To walk with short steps, rocking from side to side. ---
examples: Penguins waddle across the ice to the water.
The toddler waddled to the door in his snowsuit.
A fat goose was waddling down the middle of the path.
entries.русский: ковылять, переваливаться с ноги на ногу

entries.meaning: To avoid committing yourself, changing position or talking around the question. ---
examples: Voters punish candidates who waffle.
He waffled for a week before turning the job down.
She is still waffling about which school to accept.
entries.contrast: In American use waffle means to be indecisive; in British use it means to talk on and on without saying much.

entries.meaning: To carry on a war, a campaign, or a long struggle. ---
examples: Both parties wage the same fight every four years.
The city waged a long campaign against illegal dumping.
Health officials have been waging war on vaping in schools.
entries.contrast: Drops the -e: waging. It takes a narrow set of objects: wage war, wage a campaign, wage a battle.

entries.meaning: To cry out in a long, loud, high sound of grief or pain. ---
examples: Sirens wail all night in that neighborhood.
The child wailed until someone picked him up.
Somewhere down the block a dog was wailing.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like whale, the animal.

entries.meaning: To hit something very hard, or to beat an opponent badly. ---
examples: One good swing can wallop the ball over the fence.
The Tigers walloped the Bears 45 to 3.
He got walloped by a wave he never saw coming.
entries.contrast: The p does not double, because the stress falls on the first syllable: walloped, walloping.

entries.meaning: To cover the walls of a room with wallpaper. ---
examples: We plan to wallpaper the hallway this fall.
They wallpapered the nursery in pale green.
The kitchen had been wallpapered sometime in the 1970s.

entries.meaning: To feel that you would like to have or do something. ---
examples: They want a bigger apartment before the baby comes.
I wanted to call you, but it was already midnight.
She has always wanted to learn Spanish.
entries.contrast: Want is not normally used in the continuous: say I want it now, not I am wanting it now.

entries.meaning: To sing with a trembling sound that rises and falls, as a small bird does. ---
examples: Finches warble in the hedge all morning.
He warbled a few bars of an old show tune.
Something was warbling outside the window at five in the morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (warble a tune), intransitive (birds warble at dawn)

entries.meaning: To store goods in a warehouse, or to keep people somewhere with no real care. ---
examples: Retailers warehouse inventory near the port.
The company warehoused the parts for two years before selling them.
Critics say the state is simply warehousing the elderly.

entries.meaning: To be serious or important enough to deserve something. ---
examples: These numbers warrant a second look.
The incident warranted a full investigation.
The expense simply is not warranted by the results.

entries.meaning: To put a faint mark or image on paper or a file to show who owns it. ---
examples: Photographers watermark their previews before sending them out.
The agency watermarked every page of the draft.
The file arrived watermarked CONFIDENTIAL in gray letters.

entries.meaning: To turn something into a weapon, or to use it as a means of attacking people. ---
examples: Governments weaponize fear before an election.
Both sides weaponized the leaked emails.
The word has been thoroughly weaponized in the last few years.
entries.русский: превращать в оружие, использовать как оружие

entries.meaning: To seal and insulate a building so that it loses less heat. ---
examples: Federal grants help low-income families weatherize their homes.
We weatherized the attic before the first snow.
Older houses are rarely weatherized properly.

entries.meaning: To force something into a narrow space so that it sticks there. ---
examples: Wedge a folded napkin under the short table leg.
He wedged the door open with a brick.
Her car was wedged between a van and the curb.

entries.meaning: To make something heavier, or to give one part of a calculation more importance than another. ---
examples: Editors weight recent reviews more heavily than old ones.
The survey weighted the responses by age and region.
The final score is weighted toward the written exam.
entries.contrast: Do not confuse with weigh: you weigh a package to find out its weight, but you weight an average to change it. Past forms: weighed and weighted.

entries.meaning: To make something more like Western Europe or North America in style, dress, or institutions. ---
examples: Global chains westernize the menu wherever they open.
Reformers westernized the legal code in the 1870s.
The skyline has been thoroughly westernized in twenty years.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (westernize the curriculum), intransitive (the city has westernized fast)

entries.meaning: To hit someone or something hard with a short, sharp blow. ---
examples: Whack the lid with the flat of your hand and it will open.
He whacked the ball into the neighbor's yard.
She kept whacking the machine until it started.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (whack a nail), intransitive (whack at the weeds)

entries.meaning: To get something from someone by flattery and gentle pestering. ---
examples: Children learn early how to wheedle.
He wheedled another week out of his editor.
She was wheedling for a ride to the airport.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wheedle a favor), intransitive (stop wheedling)

entries.meaning: To push or pull something on wheels, or to turn in a wide circle. ---
examples: Nurses wheel patients down to radiology every ten minutes.
He wheeled his bike into the elevator.
Vultures were wheeling over the ridge.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wheel the cart inside), intransitive (gulls wheeled overhead)

entries.meaning: To sharpen a blade, or to make an appetite or an interest keener. ---
examples: A short trailer can whet your appetite for the film.
The first chapter whetted my curiosity.
He was whetting a knife on a stone by the fire.
entries.contrast: Doubles the t: whetted, whetting. It sounds exactly like wet, but you whet an appetite and wet a towel.

entries.meaning: To make weak, broken crying sounds. ---
examples: Puppies whimper when they are left alone.
She whimpered something about her ankle.
The child was still whimpering an hour later.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (whimper an apology), intransitive (the dog whimpered)

entries.meaning: To make a low, steady humming sound, as a fan or a small motor does. ---
examples: The ceiling fans whir all summer.
The old projector whirred and clicked in the dark.
Somewhere behind the wall a pump was whirring.
entries.contrast: Doubles the r: whirred, whirring. The spelling whirr is also correct.

entries.meaning: To make something white or paler, or to become white. ---
examples: These strips whiten teeth in about two weeks.
His knuckles whitened on the steering wheel.
The sky was already whitening in the east.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (whiten your teeth), intransitive (his knuckles whitened)

entries.meaning: To cover up something shameful so that it looks acceptable. ---
examples: Official histories whitewash the ugly parts.
The report whitewashed the department's failures.
Critics said the inquiry had been whitewashed from the start.

entries.meaning: To cut small pieces off a piece of wood in order to shape it. ---
examples: My grandfather used to whittle toys for us.
She whittled a small bird out of a block of pine.
He sat on the porch whittling the end of a stick into a point.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (whittle a spoon), intransitive (whittle by the fire)

entries.meaning: To move very fast with a rushing or buzzing sound. ---
examples: Delivery bikes whiz past the café all day.
A bullet whizzed over their heads.
Cars were whizzing by too fast to read the plates.
entries.contrast: Doubles the z before endings: whizzes, whizzed, whizzing. The spelling whizz is also used.

entries.meaning: To hold and use a tool or weapon, or to have and use power. ---
examples: Few senators wield that much influence.
The chef wielded the knife like a surgeon.
Power wielded in secret is hard to check.

entries.meaning: To move in small, quick movements from side to side. ---
examples: Can you wiggle your ears?
She wiggled the key until the lock finally turned.
He kept wiggling through the entire haircut.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wiggle your toes), intransitive (stop wiggling)

entries.meaning: To reduce a large group to the few best, or to separate grain from chaff. ---
examples: The committee will winnow the applications to ten.
Two rounds of auditions winnowed the field from sixty to eight.
The list has already been winnowed twice.

entries.meaning: To spend the winter in a particular place. ---
examples: Thousands of retirees winter in Arizona.
The herd wintered in the lower valley.
They have been wintering in Florida since he retired.

entries.meaning: To listen secretly to someone's phone calls or electronic messages. ---
examples: Agents cannot wiretap a suspect without a warrant.
The bureau wiretapped his office for six months.
He insisted that his phone was being wiretapped.
entries.contrast: Doubles the p: wiretapped, wiretapping.

entries.meaning: To move unsteadily from side to side. ---
examples: The table wobbles unless you put a shim under the leg.
Her voice wobbled on the last line of the speech.
He was wobbling badly by the end of the race.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wobble the table), intransitive (the chair wobbles)

entries.meaning: To choose the exact words in which something is expressed. ---
examples: Word the request politely and they may say yes.
She worded the apology very carefully.
The clause is worded so vaguely that nobody can enforce it.

entries.meaning: To impress someone greatly. ---
examples: This dessert will wow your guests.
She wowed the judges with a song she had written herself.
The film has wowed audiences at three festivals.
entries.русский: восхищать, приводить в восторг; произвести фурор

entries.meaning: To argue noisily and at length, or to round up and manage animals. ---
examples: Lawmakers wrangle over the same line in the budget every year.
The neighbors wrangled for months about the fence.
He spent the summer wrangling horses in Montana.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wrangle cattle), intransitive (wrangle over money)
entries.contrast: The w is silent: wrangle begins like rangle.

entries.meaning: To pull or twist something suddenly and violently. ---
examples: Do not wrench the lid; twist it slowly.
He wrenched the bag out of the thief's hand.
The gate had been wrenched off its hinges.
entries.contrast: The w is silent. A wrench is also the tool Russians call гаечный ключ.

entries.meaning: To take something away from someone by force or great effort. ---
examples: The party hopes to wrest control of the state senate.
Rebels wrested the city from the government in a week.
She has wrested confessions out of tougher witnesses than him.
entries.contrast: The w is silent, so it sounds exactly like rest. It almost always takes from.

entries.meaning: To twist and turn the body in short, quick movements. ---
examples: The puppy wriggles whenever you pick him up.
She wriggled into the back seat between the boxes.
A worm was wriggling on the wet pavement.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wriggle your toes), intransitive (the worm wriggled)
entries.contrast: The w is silent: wriggle sounds like riggle.

entries.meaning: To treat someone unjustly. ---
examples: Do not wrong the people who defended you.
He is convinced that the company wronged him.
She felt deeply wronged by the committee's decision.
entries.contrast: As a verb wrong is formal; the participle wronged is the form you meet most often (a wronged man).

entries.meaning: To pull something with one sudden, hard movement. ---
examples: Yank the cord to start the mower.
He yanked the door open and ran.
She was yanking weeds out of the flower bed.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (yank the cord), intransitive (yank on the rope)

entries.meaning: To bark in short high sounds, or to talk noisily about nothing. ---
examples: Small dogs yap at everything that passes.
The terrier yapped until we let it inside.
They were still yapping about the game at midnight.
entries.contrast: Doubles the p: yapped, yapping.

entries.meaning: To want something very much, especially something distant or lost. ---
examples: Expats yearn for food from home.
He yearned to see the coast one more time.
She had been yearning for a change for years.
entries.contrast: Takes for or to: yearn for peace, yearn to go home.

entries.meaning: To turn yellow, especially with age. ---
examples: Old paperbacks yellow at the edges.
The photographs had yellowed in their frames.
Smoke was slowly yellowing the ceiling.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the sun yellowed the blinds), intransitive (the pages yellowed)

entries.meaning: To give a short, sharp cry of pain or surprise. ---
examples: Dogs yelp when you step on a paw.
She yelped and dropped the hot pan.
He was yelping with laughter by the end of the story.

entries.meaning: To hit something with a sudden burst of energy, or to heat food quickly in a microwave. ---
examples: Zap the soup for ninety seconds.
The laser zapped the tumor in a single session.
He was zapping mosquitoes with a little electric racket.
entries.contrast: Doubles the p: zapped, zapping.

entries.meaning: To scrape the colored outer peel from a lemon, lime, or orange. ---
examples: Zest one lemon and set the peel aside.
She zested two limes for the marinade.
The oranges had already been zested and juiced.

entries.meaning: To move forward in a series of sharp turns from one side to the other. ---
examples: The trail zigzags up the face of the hill.
The skier zigzagged between the gates.
A crack was zigzagging across the ceiling.
entries.contrast: Doubles the final g: zigzagged, zigzagging.

entries.meaning: To set aside an area of a town officially for one kind of building or use.
examples: The council may zone the waterfront for housing.
They zoned the whole block for light industry in 1998.
That lot is zoned commercial, so you cannot build a house on it.
